title: Periodontology and Community Dentistry
description: Periodontal diseases and their classification, diagnosis and treatment, systemic links, and dental public health, epidemiology and oral health promotion in Nigeria.

topics.title: Periodontal Disease: Aetiology and Classification
topics.summary: Plaque biofilm, host response, risk factors, and the 2017 classification.

notes.b: Periodontal diseases are initiated by dental plaque biofilm; a dysbiotic microbiome (keystone pathogen Porphyromonas gingivalis; red complex — P. gingivalis, Treponema denticola, Tannerella forsythia; Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans in molar–incisor pattern disease) triggers a host inflammatory response that causes most of the tissue destruction (MMPs, cytokines, osteoclast activation via RANKL). Gingivitis (inflammation confined to the gingiva — bleeding on probing, redness, swelling) is reversible with plaque control. Periodontitis involves loss of connective tissue attachment and alveolar bone, pocket formation, gingival recession, mobility and eventual tooth loss; it is not reversible but can be arrested. Risk factors: smoking (the strongest modifiable factor; masks bleeding), diabetes (bidirectional relationship), genetics, stress, HIV, pregnancy (pregnancy gingivitis) and medications (gingival overgrowth — phenytoin, ciclosporin, calcium channel blockers). Local factors: calculus, overhanging restorations and crowding retain plaque.

The 2017 World Workshop classification: periodontal health; gingivitis (plaque-induced and non-plaque-induced); periodontitis — staged by severity and complexity (Stage I–IV: interdental clinical attachment loss, radiographic bone loss, tooth loss due to periodontitis, complexity factors) and graded by rate of progression and risk (Grade A slow, B moderate, C rapid — using bone loss/age ratio, smoking and diabetes modifiers); extent (localised < 30% of teeth, generalised, or molar–incisor pattern — formerly aggressive periodontitis, which is relatively common in young West Africans); necrotising periodontal diseases (NG, NP, necrotising stomatitis — associated with HIV, malnutrition and stress); periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease; and peri-implant health, mucositis and peri-implantitis. Periodontal abscesses and endo–perio lesions are also classified.

topics.title: Periodontal Diagnosis and Treatment
topics.summary: BPE, charting, radiographs, non-surgical and surgical therapy, and maintenance.

notes.b: The Basic Periodontal Examination (BPE) screens each sextant with a WHO probe (ball end; black band 3.5–5.5 mm): code 0 (healthy), 1 (bleeding), 2 (calculus or overhang), 3 (black band partly visible — pocket 3.5–5.5 mm), 4 (black band disappears — pocket > 5.5 mm), * (furcation involvement). Codes 3 and 4 lead to detailed charting: probing pocket depths, recession, clinical attachment loss, bleeding on probing, mobility (grades I–III), furcation involvement (grades I–III) and plaque scores. Radiographs (periapicals, bitewings, OPG) show bone loss pattern (horizontal, vertical/angular defects). Diagnosis combines stage, grade and extent; risk factors are recorded. Community Periodontal Index (CPI) is used in epidemiology.

Step 1: patient education and motivation, oral hygiene instruction (modified Bass toothbrushing, interdental brushes — the most effective interdental aid for open spaces, floss), risk factor control (smoking cessation, diabetes control) and supragingival plaque control. Step 2: subgingival instrumentation (root surface debridement/scaling and root planing with hand or ultrasonic instruments), with adjuncts in selected cases (systemic antibiotics such as amoxicillin plus metronidazole for grade C or molar–incisor pattern disease; chlorhexidine mouthwash short-term — stains teeth). Re-evaluation after 3 months. Step 3: periodontal surgery for residual deep pockets (access flap, regenerative procedures with barrier membranes or enamel matrix derivative for vertical defects, resective surgery, gingivectomy for drug-induced overgrowth, root coverage grafts for recession). Step 4: supportive periodontal therapy (maintenance every 3–6 months) — crucial for long-term stability. Tooth loss from periodontitis is common in older Nigerians due to limited access to care.

topics.title: Periodontal–Systemic Links and Special Conditions
topics.summary: Diabetes, cardiovascular disease, pregnancy, HIV, necrotising diseases and gingival enlargement.

notes.b: Periodontitis is associated with diabetes (poor glycaemic control worsens periodontitis; periodontal treatment reduces HbA1c by about 0.3–0.4%), cardiovascular disease (systemic inflammation, bacteraemia), adverse pregnancy outcomes (preterm birth, low birth weight, pre-eclampsia), rheumatoid arthritis (P. gingivalis citrullination), chronic kidney disease, and aspiration pneumonia in frail elderly patients. Pregnancy gingivitis and pyogenic granuloma ('pregnancy epulis') result from hormonal changes exaggerating the response to plaque. Puberty gingivitis is similar. Oral health promotion in antenatal care benefits mothers and children. Dentists should screen diabetic patients for periodontitis and refer patients with periodontitis and risk factors for diabetes screening.
k: Links with CVD, pregnancy outcomes, RA

notes.b: Necrotising gingivitis/periodontitis (punched-out papillae, pain, bleeding, halitosis, pseudomembrane; fusiform bacteria and spirochaetes; predisposed by HIV, malnutrition, stress, smoking and poor hygiene): gentle debridement, chlorhexidine or hydrogen peroxide rinses, metronidazole if systemic involvement; in malnourished children it can progress to noma. HIV-associated periodontal lesions include linear gingival erythema and necrotising periodontal disease — may be the first sign of HIV. Gingival enlargement: inflammatory, drug-induced (phenytoin, ciclosporin, nifedipine/amlodipine), leukaemic infiltration, hereditary gingival fibromatosis, and pregnancy. Gingival recession (thin biotype, traumatic brushing, orthodontic movement, periodontitis) causes sensitivity and aesthetic concerns; root coverage grafts may help. Trauma from occlusion causes mobility. Chewing sticks (e.g. Salvadora persica, orange stick) are traditionally used for oral hygiene in Nigeria and can be effective when used correctly.

topics.title: Dental Public Health and Epidemiology
topics.summary: Oral disease burden in Nigeria, epidemiological indices, and oral health care systems.

notes.b: Oral diseases (caries, periodontal disease, oral cancer, noma, dental trauma, cleft lip and palate, and tooth loss) affect billions globally and are largely preventable. In Nigeria, caries prevalence is rising with sugar consumption and urbanisation, periodontal disease is common in adults, and access to care is poor — there are very few dentists (under 5,000 for over 200 million people), concentrated in cities, with most care out-of-pocket and emergency-oriented (extractions). Epidemiological indices: DMFT/dmft (Decayed, Missing, Filled Teeth — permanent/primary; WHO index ages 5, 12, 15, 35–44, 65–74; DMFT at 12 years is the key global indicator), Community Periodontal Index (CPI), plaque and gingival indices (Silness–Löe, Löe–Silness), Dean's fluorosis index, and oral health-related quality of life measures (OHIP). WHO oral health surveys use standardised methods and calibrated examiners.

Nigeria's National Oral Health Policy (revised 2012) promotes integrating oral health into primary health care, school oral health programmes, oral health education, basic package of oral care (emergency relief of pain, ART, fluoride), and workforce development including dental therapists and dental nurses (task-sharing). The WHO Global Oral Health Action Plan (2023–2030) and the 2021 WHA resolution call for universal health coverage for oral health, reducing sugar consumption (WHO recommends free sugars < 10%, ideally < 5% of energy intake), fluoride toothpaste affordability, minimal intervention approaches, and the phase-down of dental amalgam. Common risk factor approach: oral diseases share risk factors with NCDs (sugar, tobacco, alcohol), so integrated prevention is efficient. Special groups: children, pregnant women, elderly, people with disabilities, and people living with HIV.

topics.title: Oral Health Promotion and Preventive Programmes
topics.summary: Health promotion principles, fluoride delivery, school programmes, and evaluating interventions.

notes.b: The Ottawa Charter for Health Promotion (1986) outlines five action areas: build healthy public policy (e.g. sugar-sweetened beverage tax, fluoride toothpaste standards), create supportive environments (healthy school meals, water access), strengthen community action, develop personal skills (oral health education) and reorient health services towards prevention. Health education alone produces short-term knowledge gains but rarely sustained behaviour change; upstream approaches (policy, environment) are more effective and equitable. Behaviour change models: health belief model, stages of change (transtheoretical model), and motivational interviewing. Oral health messages: brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, reduce frequency and amount of sugar, avoid tobacco and limit alcohol, and visit a dentist regularly. Messages should be culturally appropriate and delivered in local languages (Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo, Pidgin).

Fluoride works mainly topically by enhancing remineralisation, inhibiting demineralisation and bacterial metabolism. Delivery: fluoride toothpaste (most important globally; ≥ 1,000 ppm), community water fluoridation (optimal about 0.5–1.0 ppm; not practised in Nigeria), salt and milk fluoridation, varnishes, gels and mouthrinses. Excess fluoride (naturally high in some Nigerian groundwater, e.g. parts of the north and rift areas) causes dental and skeletal fluorosis; the WHO guideline for drinking water is 1.5 mg/L. School-based programmes: supervised toothbrushing with fluoride toothpaste, fissure sealant programmes, ART, oral health education and healthy school food policies. Community programmes for noma prevention (nutrition, oral hygiene, early recognition), oral cancer screening, and integration with maternal and child health services. Evaluation uses process, impact and outcome measures (e.g. changes in DMFT, plaque scores, knowledge and behaviour).
